content: A study comparing the consumption of DHA-enriched egg yolks versus non-enriched egg yolks found no significant differences in outcomes. Regarding insect-based foods, one study evaluated the effects of caterpillar cereal consumption on children aged 6–18 months, with follow-ups at 9, 12, and 18 months. The study found no impact on stunting, wasting, weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ), height-for-age z-scores (HAZ), or weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ). The evidence for these outcomes was graded as very low certainty. A cross-sectional study among children aged 6–23 months found no association between stunting and the consumption of more varied animal-source foods (ASFs) compared to less varied sources. However, no association was found with underweight status either. The evidence was rated as low to very low certainty. Another study in the same age group found no link between fish consumption frequency and stunting, wasting, or underweight, with evidence graded as very low certainty. Dietary modeling studies showed that diets minimizing nutrient gaps for 13 key nutrients included beef, lamb, game, liver, or small fish. When meat, poultry, fish, and eggs were excluded from the diets of breastfed children aged 12–23 months, gaps in iron and vitamin B12 appeared. For non-breastfed children in the same age group, vitamin B12 gaps were observed. Excluding only eggs from the diet did not affect nutrient intakes. The evidence suggests that ASF consumption improves growth outcomes, reduces anemia risk, and increases hemoglobin concentrations. Children consuming eggs from DHA-enriched chicken feed showed improved DHA status. For legumes, nuts, and seeds, evidence from two studies showed no association between legume consumption frequency and anthropometric outcomes. Similarly, daily versus less frequent consumption of beans was not associated with anemia. Dietary modeling indicated that excluding legumes, nuts, and seeds from the diet did not significantly affect nutrient intakes, as other nutrient-dense food groups compensated for the gaps. The evidence was graded as very low certainty. Regarding fruits and vegetables, six studies involving children aged 6–23 months were identified. In Senegal, fruit and vegetable consumption was positively associated with height-for-age z-scores (HAZ) and linear growth in children aged 9–23 months. However, in Norway, vegetable consumption was not associated with low iron stores. Evidence from Brazil showed no association between fruit and vegetable consumption and anemia. Dietary modeling indicated that excluding fruits did not affect nutrient intakes, but excluding vegetables reduced iron intake in all age groups. The overall certainty of evidence was very low. For starchy staple foods, dietary modeling showed that increasing their consumption in infants aged 6–11 months could prevent meeting nutrient requirements for calcium, potassium, zinc, thiamine, riboflavin, choline, and vitamin B6. Best-case diets included minimal amounts of starchy staples. The evidence on unhealthy foods and beverages, such as those high in sugar, salt, and trans fats, was of low certainty. Sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) were associated with higher BMI and dental caries in some studies, but evidence was inconsistent. Non-sugar sweeteners showed no clear association with BMI or body fat. Consumption of 100% fruit juice was not associated with adverse outcomes. Dietary modeling showed that including unhealthy foods and SSBs increased nutrient gaps, particularly for iron and zinc. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that the balance of benefits and harms favors the consumption of ASFs, fruits, and vegetables, while recommending reduced consumption of unhealthy foods and beverages. ASFs provide essential proteins, vitamins, minerals, and fatty acids, while fruits and vegetables contribute to long-term health benefits. Nuts, pulses, and seeds also offer valuable nutrients but were conditionally recommended due to limited evidence. Unhealthy foods and SSBs were deemed to have no benefits and potential harms, with recommendations favoring reduced or no consumption. Cultural and religious beliefs influence the acceptability of ASFs, with some populations excluding specific types. Fruits and vegetables are generally acceptable, but concerns about choking risks with nuts and seeds may exist. The cost of diverse diets, including ASFs and nutrient-rich foods, was noted as a barrier in some settings, with household income strongly associated with dietary diversity.
